'''Kensington''' is a [[neighborhood]] in the central portion of the [[New York City]] [[Boroughs of New York City|borough]] of [[Brooklyn]], located south of [[Prospect Park (Brooklyn)|Prospect Park]] and [[Green-Wood Cemetery]]. Kensington and Parkville are bordered by the [[Prospect Park South, Brooklyn|Prospect Park South]] and [[Ditmas Park, Brooklyn|Ditmas Park]] subsections of [[Flatbush, Brooklyn|Flatbush]] to the east; [[Windsor Terrace, Brooklyn|Windsor Terrace]] to the north; [[Borough Park, Brooklyn|Borough Park]] to the west; and [[Midwood, Brooklyn|Midwood]] to the south.

Kensington is a predominantly residential area, with housing types that include brick [[rowhouse]]s, detached one-family [[Victorian architecture|Victorians]], and apartment buildings. [[Pre-war (architecture)|Pre-war]] brick apartment buildings dominate the [[Ocean Parkway (Brooklyn)|Ocean Parkway]] and [[Coney Island Avenue]] frontage, including many that operate as [[Cooperative#Housing cooperative|co-ops]]. The neighborhood has a diverse population with residents of many ethnicities. The main commercial streets are Coney Island Avenue, Church Avenue, Ditmas Avenue, and McDonald Avenue. Ocean Parkway bisects the neighborhood east–west. Kensington's [[ZIP Code]] is 11218 and it is served by the [[New York City Police Department|NYPD]]'s 66th Precinct.<ref>{{Cite web|title=New York City Police Department|url=http://www.nyc.gov/html/nypd/html/precincts/precinct_066.shtml|access-date=July 3, 2022|website=www.nyc.gov|archive-date=June 1, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200601041439/https://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/66th-precinct.page|url-status=live}}</ref>

==History==

=== Early history ===
[[File: Kensington PO jeh.JPG|thumb|Kensington Post Office, listed on the [[List of Registered Historic Places in Kings County, New York|NRHP]]]]
The land where Kensington now sits was first colonized by Dutch farmers during the seventeenth century within the [[Flatbush, Brooklyn|town of Flatbush]]. It was re-settled by British colonists in 1737. First developed in 1885 after the completion of [[Ocean Parkway (Brooklyn)|Ocean Parkway]], the neighborhood was named after the [[Kensington|place and borough in West London]], at the turn of the century.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://beta.wnyc.org/articles/wnyc-news/2010/jul/25/ask-historian-ask-your-brooklyn-questions/ |title=Ask the Historian |access-date=July 31, 2010 |publisher=[[WNYC]] |archive-date=July 31, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100731084257/http://beta.wnyc.org/articles/wnyc-news/2010/jul/25/ask-historian-ask-your-brooklyn-questions/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The small area between 18th and Foster Avenues, in the southern portion of the neighborhood, contains a distinctive, slightly diagonal street grid and is also known as '''Parkville'''. The area, originally part of the town of Flatbush, was originally known as '''Greenville''' and its land was first acquired in 1852 by the Freeman's Association, shortly after the completion of [[Coney Island Avenue]] on the eastern boundary of Kensington and Parkville. Public School 92 (later P.S. 134) and the [[Roman Catholic]] Church of St. Rose of Lima were built to service the subsection in 1870. A librarian at the [[Brooklyn Public Library]] wrote that "Parkville is one of those wonky neighborhoods that isn't often referenced" because of its small size.<ref name=":0">{{cite web | title=What's Up With Parkville? | website=Brooklyn Public Library | date=February 18, 2015 | url=https://www.bklynlibrary.org/blog/2015/02/18/whats-parkville | access-date=October 20, 2019 | archive-date=October 20, 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191020123552/https://www.bklynlibrary.org/blog/2015/02/18/whats-parkville | url-status=live }}</ref>

Despite political tensions, the town of Flatbush was annexed by the city of Brooklyn in 1894, presaging the [[City of Greater New York|consolidation]] of the five boroughs of New York City on January 1, 1898. Accordingly, further spates of development occurred in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, much of which was initially concentrated in the village of Windsor Terrace (which had more southerly borders than the contemporary neighborhood, being bounded by Church Avenue on the south, Gravesend [McDonald] Avenue on the west, the historical Brooklyn–Flatbush town line near Terrace Place on the north, and Prospect Park Southwest and Coney Island Avenue on the east).<ref>{{Cite web |date=1890 |title=Index Map From Kings County 1890, New York |url=https://historicmapworks.com/Map/US/1600/Index+Map/Kings+County+1890/New+York/ |website=Historic Map Works}}</ref> These efforts also encompassed Brooklyn Real Estate Exchange President Jeremiah Johnson, Jr.'s circa 1891 Kensington Heights<ref>{{Cite web|title=Image 23 of Building a nation and where to build ideal American homes|url=https://www.loc.gov/resource/gdcmassbookdig.buildingnationwh00john/?sp=23|access-date=July 3, 2022|website=Library of Congress, Washington, D.C. 20540 USA|archive-date=July 3, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220703170533/https://www.loc.gov/resource/gdcmassbookdig.buildingnationwh00john/?sp=23|url-status=live}}</ref> and circa 1894 Kensington-in-Flatbush developments, the former in the vicinity of Ditmas Avenue and the latter possibly in the vicinity of Church Avenue; detached suburban villas on and adjoining Ocean Parkway that attracted wealthier residents from more urbanized areas, including [[Brooklyn Heights]], [[Bedford-Stuyvesant]] and [[Bushwick]]; hybrid commercial/walk-up apartment structures on commercial thoroughfares; and a variety of limestone- and brick-fronted townhouse rows.

=== Early and mid-20th century ===
As the area was gradually rezoned amid the construction of the [[IND Brooklyn Line]], six-story elevator apartment houses<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://dlc.library.columbia.edu/nyre/cul:d2547d7z2n|title=The Thomas Jefferson, 140 Ocean Parkway|website=Dlc.library.columbia.edu|access-date=December 6, 2021|archive-date=December 6, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211206022653/https://dlc.library.columbia.edu/nyre/cul:d2547d7z2n|url-status=live}}</ref> became increasingly prevalent on upper Ocean Parkway and in its periphery between the late 1920s and 1941, replacing many of the suburban villas.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://dlc.library.columbia.edu/nyre?utf8=%E2%9C%93&search_field=all_text_teim&q=ocean+parkway|title=The New York real estate brochure collection Search Results|website=Dlc.library.columbia.edu|access-date=December 6, 2021|archive-date=December 6, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211206022358/https://dlc.library.columbia.edu/nyre?utf8=%E2%9C%93&search_field=all_text_teim&q=ocean+parkway|url-status=live}}</ref> Following [[World War II]], the development of the [[Prospect Expressway]] ensured that luxury buildings (by now often exceeding six stories due to building code revisions and further zoning changes, as exemplified by the Marlene J. [later known as the Caton Towers]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://dlc.library.columbia.edu/nyre/cul:905qfttg92|title=The Marlene J., 135 Ocean Parkway|website=Dlc.library.columbia.edu|access-date=December 6, 2021|archive-date=December 6, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211206022511/https://dlc.library.columbia.edu/nyre/cul:905qfttg92|url-status=live}}</ref> and the Americana Towers<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://dlc.library.columbia.edu/nyre/cul:4xgxd255n9|title=Americana Towers, 455 Ocean Parkway|website=Dlc.library.columbia.edu|access-date=December 6, 2021|archive-date=December 6, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211206024322/https://dlc.library.columbia.edu/nyre/cul:4xgxd255n9|url-status=live}}</ref>) continued to be developed on Ocean Parkway and in its immediate vicinity until the mid-1960s. Since the 1990s, there has been a notable resurgence in various forms of residential development, including new apartment houses on Ocean Parkway and smaller structures on side streets.

Throughout much of the 20th century, Kensington was seldom distinguished as a distinct neighborhood, with many residents and demographers identifying the area as the western section of Beginning in the 1950s, demographic shifts in eastern Flatbush — exemplified by [[white flight]] among the Jewish American community and the concomitant emergence of an [[Afro-Caribbean]] immigrant community in the vicinity of [[Flatbush Avenue]] — would contrast with comparative stability in the Kensington tracts, notwithstanding the effects of a decade-long population decline<ref>{{Cite web |title=Search for "brooklyn communities" |url=https://www.bjpa.org/bjpa/search-results?search=brooklyn+communities |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230315004547/https://www.bjpa.org/bjpa/search-results?search=brooklyn+communities |archive-date=March 15, 2023 |website=[[Berman Jewish Policy Archive]]}}</ref> likely stemming from a variety of factors, including the beginning of post-[[Levittown, New York|Levittown]] mass [[suburbanization]] and the broader amelioration of New York City's postwar housing shortage. In 1956, the closure and ensuing "bustitution" of the [[B35 (New York City bus)|Church Avenue streetcar line]] irrevocably altered a longstanding facet of the neighborhood's public transit landscape.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.brooklynrail.net/pdf/PCC_demise_NYCTA_1956_Press_Release-1.pdf|date=1956|title=Press release|website=Brooklynrail.net|access-date=February 2, 2022|archive-date=June 27, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170627232135/http://www.brooklynrail.net/pdf/PCC_demise_NYCTA_1956_Press_Release-1.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Recognition as separate neighborhood and increasing diversity ===
Although New York City Deputy Municipal Reference Librarian Thelma E. Smith described the Kensington tracts from McDonald Avenue to Coney Island Avenue as a "sub-neighborhood" of Flatbush in a 1966 annotated bibliography of neighborhood histories and reportage for city officials,<ref>{{cite web | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SG0sAAAAMAAJ&q=mcdonald%20avenue | title=Municipal Reference Library Notes | date=August 26, 1965 | access-date=July 4, 2023 | archive-date=October 1, 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231001164858/https://books.google.com/books?id=SG0sAAAAMAAJ&q=mcdonald%20avenue | url-status=live }}</ref> ''[[The New York Times]]'' would characterize Ocean Parkway as the western boundary of Flatbush in early 1968.<ref>{{Cite news|url = https://www.nytimes.com/1968/02/14/archives/after-era-of-stability-flatbush-yields-to-change-the-talk-of.html|title = After Era of Stability, Flatbush Yields to Change; the Talk of Flatbush|newspaper = The New York Times|date = February 14, 1968|access-date = December 1, 2021|archive-date = December 1, 2021|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20211201191430/https://www.nytimes.com/1968/02/14/archives/after-era-of-stability-flatbush-yields-to-change-the-talk-of.html|url-status = live}}</ref> Shortly thereafter, the New York City municipal government informally designated the tracts between McDonald and Coney Island Avenues as Kensington in the 1969 ''Plan for New York City''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://digitalcollections.nypl.org/collections/atlases-of-new-york-city#/?tab=navigation&roots=30593990-bc6a-0132-4f30-58d385a7bbd0/28:8b252450-c603-012f-14f1-58d385a7bc34/2:f861f390-c603-012f-bea3-58d385a7bc34|title=Atlases of New York City|website=Digitalcollections.nypl.org|access-date=December 1, 2021|archive-date=December 1, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211201191430/https://digitalcollections.nypl.org/collections/atlases-of-new-york-city#/?tab=navigation&roots=30593990-bc6a-0132-4f30-58d385a7bbd0/28:8b252450-c603-012f-14f1-58d385a7bc34/2:f861f390-c603-012f-bea3-58d385a7bc34|url-status=live}}</ref> Similarly, Gilbert Tauber and Samuel Kaplan asserted that southern Windsor Terrace, the traditional Kensington tracts and western Midwood constituted the sprawling neighborhood of "Kensington-Ocean Parkway" in ''The New York City Handbook'', first published by [[Doubleday (publisher)|Doubleday]] in 1966.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://archive.org/details/newyorkcityhandb0000taub | title=The New York City handbook; a comprehensive, practical guide for natives and newcomers living and working in New York to the ins and outs of the five boroughs' assets, systems, neighborhoods, services and opportunities | date=November 19, 1966 | publisher=Garden City, N.Y., Doubleday }}</ref> (Indeed, after the contemporary [[community boards of New York City]] were established in 1963, much of present-day Kensington was appended to the [[Borough Park, Brooklyn|Borough Park]]-dominated [[Brooklyn Community Board 12]], possibly stemming from Kensington Democratic leader [[Howard Golden]]'s affiliation with Borough Park's then-powerful Roosevelt Club.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=d-UCAAAAMBAJ&dq=%22roosevelt+democratic+club%22+borough+park&pg=PA36 | title=New York Magazine | date=February 20, 1984 | access-date=June 13, 2022 | archive-date=October 1, 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231001164821/https://books.google.com/books?id=d-UCAAAAMBAJ&dq=%22roosevelt+democratic+club%22+borough+park&pg=PA36#v=onepage&q=%22roosevelt%20democratic%20club%22%20borough%20park&f=false | url-status=live }}</ref> Conversely, the eastern Flatbush and Midwood tracts were incorporated into [[Brooklyn Community Board 14]], a division that endures to the present.)

Although the formation of such community organizations as the Kensington-Flatbush Preservation Association would further popularize the moniker throughout the 1970s, press accounts continued to describe the area as Flatbush.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/464962605/?terms=%22ocean%20parkway%22%20%22flatbush&match=1 |title=2 Apr 1973, 275 – Daily News |website=Newspapers.com |access-date=December 1, 2021 |archive-date=December 1, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211201191432/https://www.newspapers.com/image/464962605/?terms=%22ocean%20parkway%22%20%22flatbush&match=1 |url-status=live }}</ref> In April 1973, Brooklyn [[Borough President]] [[Sebastian Leone]] said that planned renovations of upper Ocean Parkway (along with a smaller portion in contemporary Midwood) "[would] be an asset to the Flatbush community."<ref>{{Cite news |date=April 21, 1973 |title=Some Linear Parks For Ocean Parkway |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/465343513/?terms=%22ocean%20parkway%20in%20flatbush%22&match=1 |url-access=subscription |work=[[New York Daily News]] |location=New York City |pages=189 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> Brooklyn-born sports journalist [[Stan Fischler]] also identified the IND [[Church Avenue station (IND Culver Line)|Church Avenue]] station as being located in Flatbush in ''Uptown, Downtown'', his 1976 history of the New York City subway system.<ref>{{cite book | url=https://archive.org/details/uptowndowntowntr00fisc/page/102/mode/2up?q=flatbush | isbn=9780801531187 | title=Uptown, downtown : A trip through time on New York's subways | date=November 19, 1976 | last1=Fischler | first1=Stan | publisher=Hawthorn Books }}</ref> Reflecting this transitional milieu, the area surrounding a March 1977 gas station shootout at 417 Dahill Road was alternatively characterized as being part of Borough Park (by reporters Thomas Raftery and Paul Meskil) and as a "worn section of Flatbush" (by columnist [[Pete Hamill]]) on the same page of the ''[[New York Daily News]]''.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Raftery |first=Thomas |last2=Meskil |first2=Paul |date=March 7, 1977 |title=Slain Brooklyn Bandit Was Ex-Cop |url=https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/391597900/ |url-access=subscription |work=[[New York Daily News]] |pages=3 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref>

During this period, the Kensington tracts began to experience significant demographic changes. Most of the area's long-endangered [[mainline Protestant]] churches (including the historically prominent Prospect Park Baptist Church<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.brownstoner.com/history/past-and-present-the-prospect-park-baptist-church/ | title=Past and Present: The Prospect Park Baptist Church | date=April 12, 2013 | access-date=March 15, 2023 | archive-date=March 15, 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230315002324/https://www.brownstoner.com/history/past-and-present-the-prospect-park-baptist-church/ | url-status=live }}</ref>) were forced to close due to a lack of parishioners, while the area's deeply-rooted [[Irish American]] community continued to be supplanted by new waves of upwardly mobile Italian Americans moving out from less desirable sections of central and northern Brooklyn, paralleling developments in nearby [[Sunset Park, Brooklyn|Sunset Park]]. In a 1974 interview with Wendy Schuman of ''The New York Times'', a banker opined that Ocean Parkway "just [wasn't] prestigious anymore" as younger residents fully embraced suburbanization, leaving a substantial and rapidly aging [[white ethnic]] population (most of whom settled in the area between the early 1930s and the early 1950s)<ref>{{cite book | url=https://archive.org/details/neighborhoodsofb0000unse/page/148/mode/1up | isbn=9780300103106 | title=The neighborhoods of Brooklyn | year=2004 | last1=Jackson | first1=Kenneth T. | last2=Manbeck | first2=John B. | publisher=Yale University Press }}</ref> that proved reluctant to move due to New York's favorable rent regulation laws. Another resident who recently moved to Ocean Parkway cited the area's perceived isolation from eastern Flatbush, by now a predominantly [[Caribbean American]] community, as his impetus for relocation: "I'm a bigot. I don't care how much money they have. I'm not going to live with Blacks and Puerto Ricans. I'll move out and keep on moving. Five years ago I would have punched a guy in the nose for talking like this."<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1974/01/20/archives/change-bends-a-spine-in-brooklyn-change-bends-a-spine-of-brooklyn.html|title=Change Bends a 'Spine' in Brooklyn|newspaper=The New York Times|date=January 20, 1974|last1=Schuman|first1=Wendy|access-date=December 2, 2021|archive-date=December 2, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211202005527/https://www.nytimes.com/1974/01/20/archives/change-bends-a-spine-in-brooklyn-change-bends-a-spine-of-brooklyn.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

By the early 1980s, the Kensington designation was rapidly adopted by real estate interests as these tenants (who often identified as Flatbush residents) began to die or retire elsewhere, leading to a greater awareness of the name through a surfeit of advertising. During this period, the area became desirable to a wide range of New Yorkers (including young professionals adversely affected by [[gentrification]] in such neighborhoods as [[Park Slope]] and [[Tribeca]]; [[Orthodox Jews]], [[African Americans]] and [[Hispanic and Latino Americans]] from Borough Park, eastern Flatbush and other nearby neighborhoods; and a variety of [[Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965|post-1965 immigrant communities]], including substantial Eastern European and South Asian enclaves) as a dual locus of relatively affordable rentals amid the city's burgeoning co-op conversion movement, further entrenching the notion of Kensington as a discrete neighborhood among new residents.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Kosmer |first=John |date=December 23, 1984 |title=Goodby, loft; hello, Brooklyn |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/487127398/?terms=%22kensington%22%20%22brooklyn%22%20%22loft%22%20%22young%20professionals%22&match=1 |url-access=subscription |work=[[New York Daily News]] |location=New York City |page=255 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/485887675/?terms=%22kensington%22%20%22f%20train%22&match=1 |title=21 Apr 1981, 171 - Daily News at Newspapers.com |access-date=December 1, 2021 |archive-date=December 1, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211201191431/https://www.newspapers.com/image/485887675/?terms=%22kensington%22%20%22f%20train%22&match=1 |url-status=live }}</ref> In 1983, ''The New York Times'' described the Ocean Parkway boundary as a vestigial border in a feature about the Community Board 14 tracts of Flatbush.<ref>{{Cite news|url = https://www.nytimes.com/1983/01/30/realestate/in-you-re-thinking-of-living-in-flatbush.html|title = In You're Thinking of Living in Flatbush|newspaper = The New York Times|date = January 30, 1983|last1 = Motyka|first1 = Joan|access-date = December 1, 2021|archive-date = December 1, 2021|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20211201191431/https://www.nytimes.com/1983/01/30/realestate/in-you-re-thinking-of-living-in-flatbush.html|url-status = live}}</ref> Nevertheless, [[City College of New York]] and [[CUNY Graduate Center]] sociologist [[William B. Helmreich]] included Kensington within the boundaries of Flatbush (while acknowledging its unique demographic mix and comparatively downscale architectural profile) in ''The Brooklyn Nobody Knows'' (2016).<ref>{{Cite book|url = https://books.google.com/books?id=qGobDQAAQBAJ&q=flatbush|isbn = 9781400883127|title = The Brooklyn Nobody Knows: An Urban Walking Guide|date = October 3, 2016|publisher = Princeton University Press|access-date = March 19, 2023|archive-date = October 1, 2023|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20231001164821/https://books.google.com/books?id=qGobDQAAQBAJ&q=flatbush|url-status = live}}</ref> Additionally, members of "[[frum]]" Orthodox Jewish communities in the area frequently extend the boundaries of Flatbush to an area that corresponds to (and often exceeds) the pre-consolidation township, including contemporary Kensington and Midwood.

==Boundaries==
There are no official boundaries for New York neighborhoods.{{efn|New York City deliberately does not have official neighborhood borders, with a spokesperson for the city's planning department saying in 2023 that the city leaves the delineation "up to New Yorkers themselves."<ref name="nytimes_2023-10-29">{{cite web|last=Buchanan|first=Larry|date=October 29, 2023|url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2023/10/29/upshot/new-york-neighborhood-guide.html|title=An Extremely Detailed Guide to an Extremely Detailed Map of New York City Neighborhoods|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=December 18, 2023}}</ref>}} A 2001 ''New York Times'' article gave the borders as Caton Avenue and [[Fort Hamilton Parkway]] to the north; 36th Street, Dahill Avenue, and 47th Street to the west; Foster Avenue to the south; and [[Coney Island Avenue]] to the east.<ref name="nytimes_2001-08-05">{{cite web|last=Cohen|first=Joyce|date=August 5, 2001|url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/2001/08/05/489310.html?pageNumber=268|title=If You're Thinking of Living In/Kensington; An Old Neighborhood Is Rediscovered|work=[[The New York Times]]|page=RE5}}</ref> The 2010 edition of ''The Encyclopedia of New York City'' gives slightly different borders, moving the western boundary one block east to Macdonald Avenue, and extending the southern boundary slightly to Avenue H.<ref name="enyc_2010">{{cite book|year=2010|title=The Encyclopedia of New York City|edition=2nd|publisher=Yale University Press|isbn=978-0-300-18257-6}}</ref>

==Demographics==
Based on data from the [[2010 United States census]], the population of Kensington-Ocean Parkway was 36,891, a decrease of 46 (0.1%) from the 36,937 counted in [[2000 United States census|2000]]. Covering an area of {{convert|364.84|acres}}, the neighborhood had a population density of {{convert|101.1|PD/acre|PD/sqmi PD/sqkm}}.<ref name="PLP5">[http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p5_nta.pdf Table PL-P5 NTA: Total Population and Persons Per Acre – New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160610175331/http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p5_nta.pdf |date=June 10, 2016 }}, Population Division – [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, February 2012. Accessed June 16, 2016.</ref>

[[File:McDonald Avenue Little Bangladesh Street Sign.jpg|thumb|Little Bangladesh street sign on McDonald Avenue in 2024]]
The racial makeup of the neighborhood was 47.9% (17,686) [[White (U.S. Census)|White]], 6.9% (2,558) [[African American (U.S. Census)|African American]], 0.1% (49) [[Native American (U.S. Census)|Native American]], 24.1% (8,879) [[Asian (U.S. Census)|Asian]], 0.0% (9) [[Pacific Islander (U.S. Census)|Pacific Islander]], 0.7% (274) from [[Race (United States Census)|other races]], and 2.5% (926) from two or more races. [[Hispanic (U.S. Census)|Hispanic]] or [[Latino (U.S. Census)|Latino]] of any race were 17.6% (6,510) of the population.<ref name="PLP3A">[http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p3a_nta.pdf Table PL-P3A NTA: Total Population by Mutually Exclusive Race and Hispanic Origin – New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160610170733/http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p3a_nta.pdf |date=June 10, 2016 }}, Population Division – [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, March 29, 2011. ==Transportation==
[[File:Culver ramp from Cortelyou platform jeh.jpg|220px|left|thumb|The [[Culver Ramp]] takes the [[IND Culver Line]] from a tunnel to an elevated structure.]]
The [[New York City Subway]]'s [[IND Culver Line]] ({{NYCS trains|Culver IND north}}) runs along the western part of the neighborhood and stops underground at [[Fort Hamilton Parkway (IND Culver Line)|Fort Hamilton Parkway]] and at [[Church Avenue (IND Culver Line)|Church Avenue]]. The line rises above ground to an elevated structure ({{NYCS trains|Culver IND south}}) to serve the [[Ditmas Avenue (IND Culver Line)|Ditmas Avenue]] and [[18th Avenue (IND Culver Line)|18th Avenue]] stations.<ref>{{NYCS const|map}}</ref> In addition, Kensington is served by the {{NYC bus link|B8|B16|B35|B67|B68|B69|B103}} local buses, as well as the {{NYC bus link|BM1|BM2|BM3|BM4}} [[express bus service|express]] buses to [[Manhattan]].<ref>{{Cite NYC bus map|B}}</ref>

==Education==
===Library===
[[File:New BPL 4207 18th Av Kensington jeh.jpg|thumb|18th Avenue library]]
The Kensington branch of the [[Brooklyn Public Library]] is located at 4207 18th Avenue, near the intersection of Seton Place and East Second Street. It was originally created in 1908 as a "deposit station" with a small collection, and was located at P.S. 134, three blocks east of the current library. Within four years, it had moved twice, and in 1912, it relocated to 770 McDonald Avenue, at the southwest corner of Ditmas Avenue. The library moved again in 1960 to a location four blocks east, on 410 Ditmas Avenue, between East 4th & East 5th Streets. The current facility opened in 2012 at 4207 18th Avenue.<ref>{{cite web | title=Kensington Library | website=Brooklyn Public Library | date=August 19, 2011 | url=https://www.bklynlibrary.org/locations/kensington | access-date=February 21, 2019 | archive-date=February 21, 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190221171042/https://www.bklynlibrary.org/locations/kensington | url-status=live }}</ref><!--

Other nearby libraries include:
* The [[Windsor Terrace, Brooklyn#Library|Windsor Terrace branch]], located at East 5th Street at Fort Hamilton Parkway<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bklynlibrary.org/locations/windsor-terrace|title=Windsor Terrace Library|date=August 19, 2011|website=Brooklyn Public Library|access-date=February 21, 2019}}</ref>
* The [[Ditmas Park, Brooklyn#Library|Cortelyou branch]], located at 1305 Cortelyou Road, near Argyle Road<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bklynlibrary.org/locations/cortelyou|title=Cortelyou Library|date=August 19, 2011|website=Brooklyn Public Library|access-date=February 21, 2019}}</ref>
-->

===Schools===
Public schools in Kensington include four public primary schools: P.S. 130 (shared with Windsor Terrace), P.S. 230, P.S. 179, and P.S. 134. There are three middle schools: M.S. 839, J.H.S. 62 and J.H.S. 23. The area has no public high schools.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Mooney|first1=Jake|title=Living in Kensington, Brooklyn Name From London, People From Everywhere|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/05/25/realestate/25livi.html?pagewanted=all&_r=0|access-date=April 10, 2015|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=May 25, 2008|archive-date=February 21, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190221112431/https://www.nytimes.com/2008/05/25/realestate/25livi.html?pagewanted=all&_r=0|url-status=live}}</ref> There is also an Orthodox Jewish school called [[Yeshiva Torah Vodaas]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.torahvodaath.org/|title=Yeshiva Torah Vodaath|website=Torahvodaath.org|access-date=February 2, 2022|archive-date=February 11, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220211153206/https://www.torahvodaath.org/|url-status=live}}</ref>
